title: Correctness of an indexed store pass
statement: Fix execution limits and a program, natural numbers $c,x,y,n,T$, an expression $e$, integer-valued functions $f$ and $loc$, an initial memory $\mu$, a destination $dst$, and a state predicate $Q$. For every $j<n$, suppose $e$ is safe in the state whose locations are $loc$ updated to give variable $c$ value $j$ and whose memory is obtained by writing the first $j$ values of $f$ starting at $dst$, and that $e$ evaluates there to $f(j)$. Suppose $Q$ holds in the state with variable $c$ set to $n$ and memory containing the first $n$ values of $f$ at $dst$; the space limit is at most the word limit; $dst+n$ is at most the space limit; $loc(x)=n$; $loc(y)=dst$; $x\ne c$ and $y\ne c$; and $n(\operatorname{cost}(e)+12)+6\le T$. Then the indexed store pass using counter $c$, length expression $x$, destination expression $y$, and value expression $e$ executes from locations $loc$ and memory $\mu$ within cost $T$, ending in a state satisfying $Q$.
hypotheses_covered: For every $j<n$, $e$ is safe and evaluates to $f(j)$ in the specified state
$Q$ holds in the specified final state
Space limit is at most word limit

replaced:
Let $c,x,y,n,T,d$ be natural numbers, let $e$ be an expression, let $f$ and
$\mathrm{loc}$ be integer-valued functions on the natural numbers, let $\mu$ be an
initial memory function, let $\mathrm{dst}$ be a natural number, and let $Q$ be a
predicate on states. Fix limits and a program. For each $j<n$, suppose $e$ is safe in
the state whose local variable $c$ has value $j$ and whose memory is obtained by writing
the first $j$ values of $f$ starting at address $\mathrm{dst}$, and suppose evaluating
$e$ in that state gives $f(j)$. Suppose also that $Q$ holds in the state with local
variable $c$ set to $n$ and memory obtained by writing the first $n$ values of $f$
starting at $\mathrm{dst}$; the memory-space limit is at most the word limit;
$\mathrm{dst}+n$ is at most the memory-space limit; $\mathrm{loc}(x)=n$ and
$\mathrm{loc}(y)=\mathrm{dst}$; $x\ne c$ and $y\ne c$; and $n(\mathrm{cost}(e)+12)+6\le
T$. Then the program that initializes local variable $c$ to zero and, while
$c<\mathrm{loc}(x)$, stores the value of $e$ at address $\mathrm{loc}(y)+c$ and
increments $c$ has an execution from the state with locals $\mathrm{loc}$ and memory
$\mu$ whose cost is at most $T$ and whose final state satisfies $Q$.
